title: Well and Hymn
premise: Coral Ishikawa, a hospice nurse who has heard the dying count backwards for twenty years, comes home to find Wren — the imaginary friend who vanished when they were nine — waiting on the porch, unchanged since 1974. Wren is not a memory but a tether: something beneath the old well on Coral's family land was given a child that year, and it wants its balance restored before the harvest moon. As neighbors begin counting backwards in their sleep and the town's founding hymn plays from empty rooms, Coral uncovers what their grandmother took in 1974 — a debt paid with another family's child. To end it, Coral must descend into the well and return what was taken, choosing love for the friend who waited over the duty of silence their family kept for fifty years; Coral surfaces at moonrise hollowed but free, and Wren finally ages, one year at a time, beside them.
about_author: Vesper Thackeray is the pen name of a former rural hospice worker who spent a decade collecting the last words of the dying across three counties. They write horror about small towns that keep their promises too well.

chapters.title: The Porch Light Stays On
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. After a hospice patient counts backwards to zero and dies smiling, Coral returns to the inherited family house and finds Wren on the porch, unchanged at nine years old. The emotional beat is dread braided with tenderness — Coral's loneliness recognizing the one companion who never left, even as the well water begins to taste sweet.

chapters.title: Hymn for the Founding Choir
chapters.summary: Alternating Coral and Wren's POV. The town's descendants of the founding choir begin sleepwalking toward the well, humming a hymn no church sings anymore. Digging through her grandmother's things, Coral finds a 1974 photograph: two children by the well, one of them not Wren. The beat is investigation curdling into guilt as duty and love start pulling apart.

chapters.title: What Was Taken in 1974
chapters.summary: Coral's POV, closing with Wren's confession. Coral learns the town traded the Delgado boy to the thing below to save the harvest, and that Wren was created from his stolen voice to keep the secret singing. On harvest moon eve, the sleepwalkers ring the property. The beat is betrayal and forgiveness colliding — Wren admits he was made to lure Coral down as the final payment.

chapters.title: Counting Backwards to One
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, ending in Coral's. Wren refuses his purpose and walks Coral down into the well himself, giving back the stolen name so the thing below can finally finish its count. Coral surfaces at moonrise as the sleepwalkers wake; Wren, freed, takes his first breath of aging time. The beat is grief transmuted into chosen family — justice done outside any law, love outlasting duty.
